prize_parts.citation: For a poetic and essayistic oeuvre that renews lyric, verse narrative, elegy and the essay through a sustained encounter with classical antiquity, grief and desire, in which philological learning and formal invention work as one practice.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Anne Carson, sole credit under B004. The citation scope is narrower than in round 1, following the chair's question. The core I would rest it on is the original work: Eros the Bittersweet, Plainwater, Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox, with Men in the Off Hours and Decreation as supporting evidence of range. Translation is named only as part of the same practice, not as separate creation, and the citation does not claim that the post-2010 books equal the core. I answer the chair's common-standard question this way. For 'sustained quality across the oeuvre' I ask whether the writer keeps finding new forms in which the formal choice is what carries the feeling, so that the form is not ornament. For the 'ideal direction' in Nobel's will I ask about seriousness and depth of imaginative purpose, not subject matter. Carson meets both tests in the central books: in Nox the translating is the mourning, and in Autobiography of Red the reworked myth becomes a story of desire and difference. I apply the same tests to Cărtărescu. He is a strong candidate on imaginative depth and distinctiveness of voice, and the open question is whether the late very large novels develop or merely accumulate. I cannot answer that from translations and reception, and I will not assume it either way. On that evidence, the comparison does not make me place him above Carson. It makes the gap between them look small, as I said in round 1. Adonis remains my third position. The case I can argue from public knowledge is a poetic language remade through myth, fragmentation and a continuing dialogue with inherited Arabic forms, as in Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses. That is a different kind of ideal significance from Carson's. I cannot judge the Arabic prosody and I do not claim the case is developed. My own non-fiction practice is context only and is not evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The reservations I took into this round remain and are not resolved. First, much of Carson's effect depends on layout, typography, the book as object and a dialogue with Greek and Latin texts, so a committee reading in translation or in ordinary editions sees part of the work. Second, the corpus is concentrated and fragmentary, and the weight falls on a handful of books. Third, the best-known works may date from roughly 1998-2010. If the later books are mannered or occasional, the whole-oeuvre claim narrows to a stable core, a point Olsson and Sem-Sandberg have each made. Fourth, I have not shown that the hybrid scholarly mode fits Nobel's 'ideal direction'. I have only argued that it can, and colleagues may read the will more narrowly. Finally, I cannot rule out that Cărtărescu's claim is stronger on scale and unity of vision than I credit, because I cannot judge his Romanian prose directly. I would change my order if a closer reading showed the later Carson books to be mainly erudite play, or if the late Cărtărescu volumes were shown to develop the project and not repeat it.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He says Carson's case rests on a stable core of acknowledged texts and not on continuous development, and that mannerism is the main reason he does not put her first. He also says a Carson citation should name the poetry first.
responses.response: I accept the drafting point and have changed the citation accordingly: it now leads with lyric, verse narrative, elegy and essay, and treats translation only as part of the same practice. On the core, I agree the claim rests on a recognisable set of books, and that is why I no longer say the recent work equals them. I do not think a stable core is a failure of the whole-oeuvre standard, provided the core itself shows several different formal solutions. Eros the Bittersweet, Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox are not one gesture repeated. Your own caveat applies to your candidate in the same way: you say you cannot verify from direct reading that Cărtărescu's late novels develop. We are applying the same test and neither of us can yet settle it. I keep him as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mattson holds Cărtărescu first. She says volume cannot count for him unless the books develop, that the committee should read the late Cărtărescu volumes closely and not judge impressionistically, and that Carson's dependence on layout and design is a real limit on what a committee can assess.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. Applying your standard to Carson, the question is whether she develops, and I answer it by pointing to the different forms of her central books. Your standard has to hold for Cărtărescu as well, and you rightly say the late volumes must be read closely before any vote. On the book-object, I have narrowed the claim so that it does not rest on design. Nox is the strongest case and the one most exposed to this objection. I still think its fragments, translation notes and elegiac address carry literary weight as text. But I concede that a committee in ordinary editions may be judging a partial image. That is a real discount on Carson's case, and I weigh it. I also accept that you hold the expansive reading as open, as I hold mine.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He raises the possibility that her peak lies in roughly 1998-2010 and that some later occasional work risks mannerism. He also says Cărtărescu's long digressive structures raise a question of economy and control that Carson's concentration avoids.
responses.response: Your qualification about the later work is the one that has changed my drafting. I have kept the citation to the established core and I do not claim development after roughly 2010. I cannot confirm from public knowledge how the later books compare. On economy, I think Carson's concentration is a real advantage in what a committee can verify, but I would not treat economy as sufficient merit. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg argue that the digressions are a method, and I cannot refute that without reading Romanian. I would hold the economy point as a reservation about Cărtărescu, not as a reason to dismiss him. Where I would press you is on Adonis, whom you also keep as an alternative. The chair has asked for a literary case for him, and I have given what public knowledge supports while saying I cannot judge his Arabic prosody.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first. She weighs repeated invention of new forms above the scale of a single vision, and she reads the 'ideal direction' through what the work does and not its genre. She also says the case holds only if emotional and imaginative depth is what readers carry away.
responses.response: I share your reading of the 'ideal direction' and I use the same test, which is why I name grief and desire in the citation. I would qualify your weighting of range over scale. Range alone is not a criterion, and Mattson and Sem-Sandberg are right that a single coherent cosmology realised at novel scale is a different and legitimate kind of achievement. My reason for preferring range is narrower: it is easier for me to verify in English. That is a limit on my knowledge and not an argument that Carson's kind of achievement outranks Cărtărescu's. Your condition that emotional depth must be what readers carry away is the one that the later Carson books must be tested against.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Carson first. She would anchor the citation in original poetry and essays and name The Beauty of the Husband and Plainwater among the works, and she concedes that some later books may be occasional. She also says her agreement should not cover over the question of how the will is read.
responses.response: I have adopted your anchoring: the core works I name are original books, and translation appears only as part of the same practice. I agree that agreement on Carson should not paper over the reading of the will. Four members prefer her, but that is not evidence of literary merit, and I do not treat it as such. If a colleague reads 'idealistic' more narrowly, the dispute should be argued on literary grounds with the same test applied to every shortlisted writer. You and I both flag that a reader judging in translation cannot fairly weigh Carson's English against Romanian or Arabic texture. I think that is the most important uneven-information problem in this comparison, and I would not hide it by treating the two leading cases as equally well read.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text. My assessment rests on general public knowledge of the major books and on the colleagues' stated readings.
How much of Carson's effect, especially in Nox and other design-dependent books, survives translation and ordinary editions is unresolved.
Whether Carson's work after roughly 2010 keeps the level of the core is unverified, and my citation deliberately does not claim it.
Whether the late large Cărtărescu novels develop or repeat earlier motifs cannot be settled from translations and reception, and I cannot read Romanian sentence texture.
Whether a hybrid scholarly-poetic mode meets Nobel's 'ideal direction' depends on how the committee reads the will, and a narrower reading is reasonable.
Translation limits for Arabic prosody (Adonis) and French sentence texture (Michon) mean the comparisons with B044 and B015 are provisional and unevenly informed.

Carlberg's actual committee voting status is undocumented, so this simulated vote is a modeling assumption and is not a record of real influence. The simulated recommendation does not replace the decision of the full Swedish Academy.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, professional or family connection to Anne Carson, Mircea Cărtărescu, Adonis or any other shortlisted writer. Her institutional ties are to Swedish Academy colleagues, including Steve Sem-Sandberg, who was elected alongside her in 2020. Her spouse's public career (former finance minister) has no documented link to any shortlisted writer. Her own archival non-fiction practice is context only. As Permanent Secretary since 1 June 2026 she may be expected to announce the laureate, which is an institutional role and not a connection to any candidate. The profile does not say whether she votes in committee.
